blocks.x: Why smart access is getting attention

More new housing is opening in Winnipeg. Housing completions were up 52.7% in the first seven months of 2026, the [City of Winnipeg](https://www.winnipeg.ca/news/2026-08-20-winnipeg-leads-major-canadian-cities-housing-growth) reports. Some rental buildings here already [list keyless entry among their amenities](https://www.broadstreet.ca/manitoba/winnipeg/edgewood-place), which puts smart locks for rental properties on the list for older buildings too.
For landlords and property managers, smart access can also solve real operational problems:
**Less rekeying** when tenants move out.
**Easier access for maintenance staff,** with time-limited codes, within the entry rules below.
**Audit trails** showing who entered and when.
**Fewer lockouts** and after-hours calls.
Owners of older buildings may see the appeal, especially with [Winnipeg one-bedroom asking rents down three months in a row](https://liv.rent/blog/?p=69631) as of October 2026.
Why smart locks fail on old rental doors
Smart locks are precision devices. Their motors and sensors expect a door that closes smoothly and aligns properly with the strike. Common problems in older buildings include:
**Sagging or warped doors** that need pushing or lifting to latch.
**Worn or damaged frames,** often from years of forced entry or repairs.
**Old bore holes and hardware cut-outs** that do not match modern locks.
**Hollow-core doors** that are not strong enough for heavier hardware.
**Poor weatherstripping** that adds friction and can make motorized bolts fail.
When smart locks are installed on poor doors, the result can be battery drain, jammed bolts, false alarms and tenant frustration. The technology gets blamed for a carpentry problem.
Our view: treat the door as part of the system
A reliable smart-access project starts with a door assessment. For each opening, ask:
Does the door close and latch without force?
Is the frame solid and square?
Is the door strong enough (solid core or insulated steel) for the hardware?
Are existing preparations compatible with the planned lock?
Does the door seal properly against drafts?
Where the answer is no, replacing the door and frame before installing new hardware can cost less than fighting recurring service calls.
What professional residential door installation covers
Professional [residential door installation](/services/windows-and-doors) for a smart-access upgrade typically includes:
**Removing old doors and frames** where needed.
**Installing new pre-hung doors** that are square, plumb and properly shimmed.
**Preparing doors for the chosen hardware,** or ordering factory-prepped doors.
**Weatherstripping and thresholds** for exterior doors.
The electronic side is separate. Your access-control provider usually installs and programs those components, so agree who does what before you order.
Because Winnipeg winters are hard on exterior doors, insulated steel or fibreglass doors with good seals are a sensible choice for building entrances.
Fire, code and tenancy rules

In apartment buildings, suite entry doors are often part of the fire separation. Replacing them may require fire-rated doors, frames and self-closing hardware. Any changes to building entrances should also consider accessibility.

Property managers should check requirements with the City's permit office, or the local authority outside Winnipeg, before ordering hardware, and work with installers familiar with code requirements. Ask whether new hardware or holes affect a door's rating.

The City's [commercial alteration guide](https://legacy.winnipeg.ca/ppd/Documents/Permits/CommercialAlterationDesignSummary/Guide-Commercial-Alteration-Design-Summary.pdf) notes that exit doors must open from the inside without keys, special devices or specialized knowledge, so ask how any electronic lock behaves in a fire or when the power or battery fails.

Tenancy rules still apply. Under [Manitoba's Residential Tenancies Act](https://web2.gov.mb.ca/laws/statutes/ccsm/r119.php), neither a landlord nor a tenant may change a suite's lock without the other's consent, and consent can't be unreasonably withheld. Changes to a building's entry can't unreasonably block access either. A code also does not change [when a landlord can enter](https://www.gov.mb.ca/cca/rtb/resource_list/privacy.pdf).

The Residential Tenancies Branch's fact sheet generally calls for 24 hours to two weeks of written notice, and says landlords should go with outside contractors to let them in. Think about tenant privacy before you keep entry logs. This is general information, not legal advice, so check with the Branch.
A phased approach
**Start with the main entrance**, where access control delivers the most value.
**Upgrade suite doors** at turnover, so tenants are not disrupted.
**Standardize hardware** across the building to simplify maintenance.
**Track service calls** to confirm the upgrade is working.
A simple comparison

Consider a building where some smart locks keep generating service calls because doors do not latch properly. Each call costs staff time and frustrates tenants, and a straining bolt drains batteries faster. Replacing the worst doors and frames, before or alongside the lock rollout, can cost less over a few years than repeated service calls and premature hardware replacement.
The same logic applies to building entrances: a poorly fitted main door can defeat any access-control system, while a well-fitted door helps make it reliable.
The bottom line
Keyless entry is appearing in new rental buildings, and it can save landlords time and money. But the technology depends on the basics.

Doors that are solid, square, well sealed and properly prepared make smart hardware reliable, while worn doors and frames turn it into a source of complaints. Start with a door assessment, replace the worst openings, and then install the hardware.
